# `unsigned-comparison-constant`

<!-- rule-docs:header (generated by `zig build rule-docs`) -->
Tier: correctness · Profile: none · Default: warning · Fixes: none · Options: none

Reports `x >= 0` (always true) and `x < 0` (always false), or the mirrored
forms, when `x` is proven unsigned by its declared type, a `for` range capture,
or `.len`.
<!-- /rule-docs:header -->

## Why it matters

An unsigned value is never negative, so `x >= 0` is always true and `x < 0` is
always false. The comparison compiles, but the branch it guards always or
never runs, and the check the author meant is missing: often the value was
meant to be signed, the bound should have been `> 0`, or a different operand
was meant. A guard such as `if (index >= 0 and index < len)` reads as a bounds
check while only half of it does anything.

## When it fires

It reports `x >= 0`, `x < 0`, `0 <= x` and `0 > x` when `x` is proven unsigned
by its spelling: a local, parameter or constant declared with an unsigned
primitive type (`u8`, `u32`, `usize`, `c_uint`, ...), the index capture of a
`for` range (`for (items, 0..) |item, index|`), a `.len`, or a builtin such as
`@sizeOf` or `@intFromPtr`. Values whose type comes from a generic parameter
or another declaration are not judged.

It does not report a comparison marked `comptime`, the whole argument of an
`assert` call (`assert(level >= 0)` beside `assert(level < max)` documents the
range on purpose), or the condition of a descending
`while (index >= 0) : (index -= 1)` loop, which `unsigned-reverse-loop`
reports.

<!-- rule-docs:footer (generated by `zig build rule-docs`) -->
## Example

```zig
fn hasItems(items: []const u8) bool {
    return items.len >= 0;
}
```
